verdict.rationale: Cal.com documents a self-hostable MIT-licensed edition, Cal.diy, that needs no license key, so self-hosting is a first-party capability. However, Cal.diy is a fork with the enterprise code removed: community reports say it drops Teams, Organizations, Workflows and SSO, is recommended only for personal, non-production use, and no longer ships public Docker images. missing for 10: self-hosting of the full core product including team/org/workflow features, production-supported self-host deployment, prebuilt Docker images, first-party self-hosting install docs.

support.subject: As an AI-native user, I can self-host the core product

citations.quote: Cal.com's differentiators are the self-hostable MIT edition (Cal.diy)
It's designed for individuals and self-hosters who want full control over their scheduling infrastructure
a fork of Cal.com with all enterprise/commercial code removed.
No license key required — Everything works out of the box, no Cal.com account or license needed
